parts.intro: You will hear a man phoning a bike hire company to book a family cycling tour.

turns.text: Good morning, Riverside Wheels, bike hire and guided tours. Lucy speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hi. I'm calling because I'd like to book one of your family cycling tours. We're visiting the area in the summer, and my kids are really excited about the idea.
Lovely. I can take the booking over the phone now, if you like. Could I start with your name?
Sure. It's Daniel Tremayne.
And could you spell the surname for me?
Yeah, it's T-R-E-M-A-Y-N-E.
Thank you. And which tour were you interested in? We've got three family routes at the moment.
Well, I was looking at your website, and the Castle Trail looked amazing, but I see it's about thirty kilometres.
That's right, it's our longest. It takes most of the day, so it's really better for older teenagers.
Yeah, I think that would be too much for us. What about the one that goes along the river?

The River Loop? I'm afraid that one's closed this summer, because they're repairing one of the bridges. But the Orchard Trail is very popular with families. It's completely flat, it's about twelve kilometres, and you stop at a fruit farm halfway round.
That sounds perfect. Let's go for the Orchard Trail.
Great. And what date would you like?
We were thinking of Thursday the 14th of August.
Let me just check. Oh, I'm sorry, the 14th is fully booked. I could offer you Saturday the 16th, or there's space on the 21st.
The 21st is too late, we fly home on the 20th. So, the 16th, please.
Fine, I've put you down for the 16th. How many people will there be?
There's my wife and me, and our three children.
And how old are the children? We need to know so we can give everyone the right size of bike.
The two older ones are eleven and nine, and they're both pretty confident riders. But our youngest, Rosie, is only five.
Ah, then she'll need some extra equipment. We can either attach a trailer to one of the adult bikes, or fit a child seat on the back.
Hmm. I think she'd feel a bit shut in, in a trailer. She likes to sit up and see what's going on, so a seat, please.
No problem, I'll make a note of that. Now, the tour starts at half past nine, and we meet in the town centre.
At your shop?
Well, the shop is actually quite small, so the guides meet the groups outside the library on Market Street. It's opposite the bus station, so it's easy to find.
Outside the library. Got it.
And can you tell me how much it's all going to cost?
Of course. Adults are 44 pounds each, and children with their own bikes are 22 pounds. Your youngest doesn't pay for the tour itself, but there's a charge of 10 pounds for the child seat.
So that's 88 for my wife and me, 44 for the older two, and then 10 for the seat.
Yes, so 142 pounds altogether.
Is there a family discount at all? I think I saw something about that online.

There was one last year, but I'm afraid we've stopped it. The price does include quite a lot, though. Everyone gets a helmet, of course, and a bottle of water, and each family gets a guidebook with information about the places you pass.
Oh, that's nice. What about lunch?
Lunch isn't included, but the fruit farm has a lovely café, and it's not expensive.
OK. And is there anything we need to bring with us?

Comfortable shoes and sun cream, definitely. And the weather here can change very quickly, even in August, so please bring a raincoat for each person. We do sell them in the shop, but they're quite expensive.
Right, I'll make sure we pack them.

And finally, to confirm the booking, we ask for a deposit of 30 pounds, which you can pay on our website. We normally give people a week to pay, but because it's the busy season, we'll need it by Friday.
By Friday. You mean this Friday?
That's right. If we haven't received it by then, the places will be offered to other customers.
No problem, I'll do it this evening. Thanks so much for your help.
You're welcome, Mr Tremayne. I hope you all enjoy the tour.

parts.intro: You will hear a woman talking on a local radio programme about a volunteer programme in a city park.

turns.text: Good afternoon, and thank you for inviting me onto the programme. My name's Helen Ashby, and I coordinate the volunteers at Greenhollow Park, which, as many of your listeners will know, opened on the site of the old railway yards last spring.

Now, a lot of people assume that the park is run entirely by the city council. In fact, the council owns the land, but the day-to-day running is shared between a small paid team and a charitable trust, and it's the trust that's launching our new volunteer programme this month.

So why now? Well, the park has been far more popular than anyone predicted. We expected around two thousand visitors a week, and we're actually getting nearer five thousand at weekends alone. That's wonderful, of course, but it does mean that the paths and the planting are wearing out faster than our team can repair them. Money isn't really the issue, by the way. We were given a generous grant in the summer. It's simply that there aren't enough hands.

So, who can volunteer? We welcome anyone over sixteen, and younger teenagers are welcome to come along with a parent. You don't need any gardening experience at all; we'll teach you everything. What we do ask is that you can commit to at least one session a month for six months, because training each new volunteer takes up quite a lot of our staff's time.

Sessions run on Tuesday and Thursday mornings, and on Saturdays from ten until one. We did think about evening sessions, but in winter it's simply too dark to work safely. Each session begins with a short safety talk, and we provide all the tools, as well as gloves and waterproof jackets. The one thing we can't provide is footwear, so please don't turn up in trainers. You'll need to bring suitable boots.

There's a social side to all this, too. Once a month, after the Saturday session, there's a shared lunch in the park café, and in December we hold a celebration evening, where we give awards to the volunteers who've contributed the most. But when we asked our first group of volunteers what they valued most, the answer was something else entirely: they told us it was learning practical skills that they could use in their own gardens.
Now, I'd like to tell you about the areas where volunteers will be working this autumn. If you have a look at the map on our website, you'll see that the park is divided into five main zones.

First, the Wildflower Meadow. People often think we just leave it to grow wild, but at this time of year the grass has to be cut. We can't use machines there, because of the birds that nest on the ground, so volunteers will be cutting back the plants by hand. It's hard work, but very satisfying.

Next, the Lake. The ducks and geese are doing very well, and we did consider asking volunteers to count the birds there, but a local wildlife group already does that every month. What we really need on the lake is help removing the rubbish that blows into the water. We provide long-handled nets for that, and you'll be amazed what you find.

In the Children's Garden, you might expect the job to be planting, and there will be some of that in the spring. But this autumn the priority is the wooden fences around the vegetable beds, which were badly damaged in the storms, so volunteers will be repairing those.

The Orchard is only two years old, so I'm afraid there isn't enough fruit to pick yet. Instead, the main job will be planting bulbs under the trees, mostly daffodils, so that the orchard is full of colour in March.

And finally, the Woodland Walk. The paths there are in good condition, so they won't need any work this year. However, the university has asked us to help them keep a record of the bats and owls that live in the wood, so volunteers there will be taking part in a wildlife survey. That's the one exception to our daytime rule, as it starts in the early evening.
If you'd like to join us, the easiest way is to fill in the short form on the trust's website, and we'll invite you to an introductory morning. We'd love to see you there.

parts.intro: You will hear two students, Sophie and James, discussing their presentation on marine plastic waste with their tutor.

turns.text: Come in, both of you, and have a seat. So, you wanted to talk about your presentation on marine plastic. How's it going?
Well, we've done most of the reading, but we're still not completely sure what the focus should be.
Yeah, at first we wanted to cover everything: where the plastic comes from, what happens to it in the ocean, the effects on wildlife, possible solutions.
That's a lot for fifteen minutes.
Exactly. We timed a practice run last week and we were nearly half an hour over, so now we're thinking we should concentrate on the sources, where the plastic actually comes from.
I think that's sensible. And, to be honest, most groups go straight for the wildlife pictures, turtles and so on, so looking at sources would make yours stand out.

One thing that really surprised me was that most of the plastic in the sea doesn't come from ships. I'd always assumed it did. But according to most estimates, around eighty percent of it comes from the land, carried by rivers or blown off rubbish sites.
That's a good point to open with, because I suspect your audience will make the same assumption. Where are you getting your data from?
Mostly from journal articles. We did find a documentary that looked useful, but some of its figures were quite old, so we've decided not to rely on it.
Good. Always check the date of every statistic you use. Now, how are you planning to divide the work?
I'm better at the visual side of things, so I was going to design the slides, and Sophie would do most of the talking.
Hmm. Actually, I should mention that we assess each person's speaking, so you'll both need to present for roughly equal amounts of time.
Oh, I didn't realise that. OK, so we'll split the talking, and James can still design the slides.
Fine. And what about the ending? That's often the weakest part of a presentation.
We thought we'd finish with a summary of the main points.
That's fine, but you could make it more memorable. What if you ended by asking the audience to think about the plastic they've used that day?
Oh, I like that. It makes it personal.
Yeah, let's do that instead of the summary.
So, within the land-based sources, which ones are you actually going to talk about?
We'd like to pick the less obvious ones. Everyone already knows about plastic bags and drinks bottles, so we're going to skip those.
The two we found really interesting were car tyres. Tiny pieces wear off them on the road and then get washed into drains.
And synthetic clothes. Every time you wash a fleece jacket, thousands of tiny fibres go down the drain and end up in rivers.
Both excellent choices. What about fishing nets? There's a lot of research on those.
They're important, but they're lost at sea, so they're not land-based. We'll leave them out.
Fair enough. Now, you mentioned some sources you're going to use. Let's go through them.
Well, first there's a survey by a beach clean-up group. Their volunteers recorded every item they found over a whole year.
Those surveys can be useful, but they're not always consistent in their methods.
True. We were going to build the whole talk around it, but I think we'll just mention it in passing.
Then there's the report on tyre dust from a transport research institute. It has really clear data.
Yes, and there's a fantastic photograph in it of the particles under a microscope. Could we use that?
You could, as long as you credit it. But the numbers are what matter. I'd suggest you turn them into a chart of your own; it'll be much easier for the audience to follow than a table full of figures.
OK, so we'll make a chart from it.
And finally, there's the laundry study, the one where they measured the fibres released by different fabrics.
That's the most recent research you have, isn't it?
Yes, it was published this year. Actually, I think that should be our main example. The results are so striking.
Agreed. We'll spend most of the second half on it.
Sounds like a plan. Send me your slides by next Wednesday and I'll give you some feedback.

parts.intro: You will hear a lecture about the psychology of habit formation.

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture, I'm going to look at the psychology of habits: what they are, how they develop in the brain, and what research tells us about changing them. This is a topic with obvious practical applications, from public health campaigns to personal productivity, but today I want to concentrate on the underlying mechanisms rather than on advice.

Let's begin with a definition. Psychologists generally describe a habit as a behaviour that is triggered automatically by a particular context, without conscious deliberation. The crucial word here is 'automatically'. When you first learn to drive, every action requires your full attention. After a few months, you can drive home while thinking about something else entirely. The behaviour itself hasn't changed, but the mental effort it requires has fallen dramatically.

So how does this transition happen? Most researchers describe a three-part cycle. First, there's a cue, which might be a location, a time of day, an emotional state, or the presence of particular people. Second, there's the routine, which is the behaviour itself. And third, there's the reward, some pleasant consequence that makes the behaviour more likely to be repeated. Each time the cycle is completed, the association between the cue and the routine becomes a little stronger.

Neuroscientific studies suggest that, as a habit forms, control of the behaviour gradually shifts from the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in planning and decision-making, to a deeper structure called the basal ganglia. This shift is efficient, because it frees the prefrontal areas for other tasks. But it also helps to explain why habits are so persistent: they are stored in a region of the brain that operates largely outside our awareness.

How long, then, does it take to form a habit? You may have come across the popular claim that it takes exactly twenty-one days. In fact, there's very little evidence for this figure, which seems to have originated in anecdotes rather than in experiments. In one influential type of study, volunteers chose a simple daily behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water after breakfast, and reported each day how automatic it felt. On average, it took more than two months to reach the point where the behaviour felt as automatic as it ever would, and the range was enormous: some participants got there within three weeks, while others took most of a year. Not surprisingly, more complex behaviours, like going to the gym, took considerably longer than simple ones. One encouraging finding, however, was that missing a single day made very little difference to the overall process. So perfection isn't required.

What about breaking unwanted habits? Here the research is rather more sobering. Simply deciding to stop is usually not enough, because the cue continues to trigger the old routine automatically. Willpower, it turns out, is a limited resource, and people who rely on it alone tend to relapse, particularly when they're tired or under stress.

A more effective strategy is to alter the environment so that the cue no longer appears at all. Studies of people who had recently moved house found that this was an ideal moment to change behaviour, since many of the old cues had simply disappeared. Researchers refer to this as the 'discontinuity' effect. For instance, people who had moved were considerably more likely to begin commuting by bicycle, provided that they already cared about the environment.

Another approach is substitution: keeping the same cue, but attaching a different routine to it. Someone who always snacks while watching television, for example, might replace the snack with a glass of water or a short stretching exercise. This tends to work better than trying to suppress the behaviour completely, because the cue still leads somewhere, and the brain isn't left with an empty gap.

Finally, it's worth noting that habits are not inherently good or bad. The same mechanism that makes it hard to give up sugary drinks also makes it possible to brush our teeth or fasten a seatbelt without thinking. In the next lecture, we'll look at how governments and health organisations have tried to use these findings, and at some of the ethical questions that raises.

texts.title: The return of the urban tram

paragraphs.text: In the first half of the twentieth century, trams were a familiar sight in hundreds of cities across Europe, North America and Australia. Running on rails laid into the street and drawing power from overhead wires, they carried millions of passengers to work, school and market every day. Yet by the 1960s most of these networks had vanished. In city after city, tracks were torn up or simply covered with asphalt, and the tram came to be regarded as a slow, noisy relic of an earlier age. Today, remarkably, the tram is back. Since the mid-1980s more than a hundred new systems have opened worldwide, and many more are under construction or at the planning stage.

The decline of the first generation of trams had several causes. The most obvious was the rapid spread of private car ownership after the Second World War. As streets filled with traffic, trams sharing the road with cars were frequently delayed, and their reliability suffered. Motor buses, meanwhile, offered transport authorities a cheaper alternative: they required no tracks and no overhead power lines, and their routes could be altered overnight in response to changes in demand. Many tram operators had also failed to invest in their vehicles and infrastructure, so that by the 1950s passengers were often travelling in carriages that were several decades old. Faced with the cost of replacing worn-out track, numerous city councils concluded that abandoning the system altogether was the more sensible option.

Not every city followed this path, however. A number of cities in central Europe, particularly in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands, chose to modernise their networks rather than close them. Engineers there developed longer, articulated vehicles that could carry far more passengers than their predecessors, and planners began to give trams their own lanes, physically separated from general traffic. These cities would later serve as models when planners elsewhere began to reconsider the value of rail-based street transport.

The revival that began in the 1980s was driven by a combination of practical and environmental concerns. Traffic congestion in city centres had reached levels that were costly in both economic and human terms, and air quality had become a serious public health issue. Because trams are powered by electricity, they produce no exhaust fumes at street level, and if that electricity comes from renewable sources, their overall emissions can be very low indeed. Trams also have a considerably greater capacity than buses: a single modern vehicle can carry over three hundred people, roughly three times as many as a standard articulated bus. On busy routes, this translates into fewer vehicles, fewer drivers and lower operating costs over time.

Supporters of trams also point to a less tangible benefit, which transport researchers sometimes refer to as the 'rail factor'. Surveys in several countries have suggested that people are more willing to use a tram than a bus, even when the two services offer identical journey times. One explanation is that the fixed tracks give passengers a sense of permanence: they can see exactly where the route goes and trust that it will not be withdrawn the following year. Trams also tend to offer a smoother, quieter ride, and their level boarding, with the vehicle floor at the same height as the platform, makes them easier to use for people with pushchairs, wheelchairs or heavy luggage.

There is also evidence that a new tram line can stimulate investment along its route. Property developers, confident that the line will remain in place for decades, are more willing to build homes, offices and shops near the stops. In several French cities, the construction of a tram network was deliberately combined with the redesign of public spaces, with wide pavements, trees and pedestrian squares replacing what had previously been multi-lane roads. Critics, however, argue that the economic benefits attributed to tram schemes are often overstated, and that similar regeneration might well have taken place without them.

The greatest obstacle to new tram systems remains their cost. Laying track involves relocating the water pipes, gas mains and cables buried beneath the street, work that is slow, disruptive and expensive. Construction can close roads for months, and local businesses frequently complain of lost trade. For this reason, some cities have turned to an alternative known as 'bus rapid transit', in which high-capacity buses run in dedicated lanes, achieving some of the advantages of trams at a fraction of the price. Engineers are also experimenting with new technology to reduce costs: some recent vehicles carry batteries that allow them to run for short distances without overhead wires, which is particularly useful in historic city centres, where the wires are considered unsightly.

Whether the tram revival continues will depend largely on how cities weigh these immediate costs against long-term benefits. What is clear is that a form of transport once dismissed as obsolete has earned a second chance, and that its future may prove considerably brighter than its past.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Deserts cover roughly a third of the Earth's land surface, and they are defined not by heat but by a shortage of water: most receive less than 250 millimetres of rainfall a year, and some receive almost none for years at a time. To a plant, such conditions present an extraordinary challenge. Plants need water not only to grow but also to carry out photosynthesis, the process by which they use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide into sugars. Yet every time a plant opens the tiny pores on its leaves, known as stomata, to take in carbon dioxide, water vapour escapes. In a hot, dry atmosphere, this loss can prove fatal within hours.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One group of desert plants has solved the problem by avoiding drought altogether. These are the so-called ephemerals, annual plants whose seeds may lie dormant in the soil for many years. When sufficient rain finally falls, the seeds germinate, and the plants grow, flower and produce a new generation of seeds within a few weeks, before the soil dries out again. The seeds themselves are remarkably sophisticated. Many contain chemical inhibitors that are washed away only by a substantial quantity of rain, which prevents them from germinating after a light shower that would not provide enough moisture for the plant to complete its life cycle.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Perennial plants, which must endure the dry season rather than avoid it, have developed a wide range of structural adaptations. The most familiar are the succulents, such as cacti, which store water in thick, fleshy stems or leaves. A large cactus may hold several hundred litres of water, enough to sustain it through months of drought. Many succulents have pleated or ribbed stems that expand like an accordion as they absorb water after rain and contract as the stored water is used. Their surfaces are typically coated with a waxy layer that greatly reduces evaporation, and their leaves have often been reduced to spines, which lose almost no water and also deter thirsty animals.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other perennials rely instead on reaching water that lies deep underground. The roots of certain desert shrubs have been found at depths of more than fifty metres, where they tap into permanent groundwater. Such plants are known as phreatophytes, and their survival depends less on rainfall than on the level of the water table. Cacti, by contrast, usually have shallow but extensive root systems that spread out just below the surface, allowing them to collect water rapidly from even a brief storm. Within hours of rain, some species grow fine new 'rain roots', which wither again once the soil dries.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most ingenious adaptations, however, are invisible to the naked eye. Many succulents use a modified form of photosynthesis known as crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, named after the plant family in which it was first studied. CAM plants keep their stomata closed during the heat of the day and open them only at night, when temperatures are lower and the air is more humid. Carbon dioxide absorbed in darkness is stored in the form of an acid, and then released inside the leaf during daylight hours, when the plant can use the energy of the sun to turn it into sugar. The trade-off is that CAM plants generally grow very slowly, but they may lose as little as a tenth of the water that conventional plants lose for the same amount of carbon gained.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some desert plants have even found ways to harvest moisture from the air. In coastal deserts, where fog drifts inland from the ocean, certain grasses and shrubs have leaves whose surfaces cause tiny droplets to collect and run down towards the roots. Researchers have examined these surfaces in detail in the hope of designing materials that could collect drinking water in arid regions, and early prototypes inspired by such plants have produced encouraging results in field trials.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Despite these remarkable adaptations, desert vegetation is more fragile than it appears. Because plants grow so slowly, damage caused by vehicles, overgrazing or construction can take decades to repair, and some slow-growing species may never recover in the affected area. Climate change poses a further threat: higher temperatures accelerate evaporation, and shifting rainfall patterns may disrupt the precise signals on which ephemeral seeds depend. Scientists warn that some desert ecosystems, which have persisted for thousands of years, could be transformed within a single human lifetime.

texts.title: Measuring happiness: the economics of well-being

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, governments measured national progress almost exclusively in terms of economic output. Gross domestic product, or GDP, which sums the market value of all goods and services produced in a country, became the dominant yardstick by which policies were judged and nations compared. Its appeal is easy to understand: it is precise, comparable across countries and years, and closely linked to employment and tax revenue. Yet even the economists who devised it cautioned that it was never intended to serve as a measure of welfare. GDP rises when a country rebuilds after a flood, when traffic congestion increases fuel consumption and when people spend more on treating preventable illnesses. It assigns no value to unpaid care, to leisure, or to the condition of the natural environment.

Dissatisfaction with GDP as a proxy for progress has given rise to a rapidly expanding discipline sometimes described as the economics of well-being. Its central proposition is deceptively simple: if we wish to know how people's lives are going, we should ask them. Large-scale surveys now routinely invite respondents to rate their satisfaction with life on a scale from nought to ten, or to estimate how much of the previous day they spent feeling contented, anxious or bored. Sceptics initially dismissed such data as hopelessly subjective, but researchers have found that the responses are surprisingly consistent. Individuals who report high life satisfaction are also rated as happier by their friends and relatives, smile more frequently in conversation, and are less likely to develop a range of stress-related illnesses.

Among the earliest and most contested findings concerns the relationship between income and happiness. Within any given country, at any given moment, wealthier people tend to report greater life satisfaction than poorer people. Yet an influential study published in the 1970s observed that, over several decades during which average incomes had risen substantially, average reported happiness in the United States had scarcely altered. One explanation is that people evaluate their circumstances largely in relative terms: what matters is not how much one earns, but how much one earns compared with neighbours, colleagues and one's own expectations. As a society grows more prosperous, the reference point rises accordingly, and the anticipated gain in satisfaction is cancelled out. Subsequent research using larger international data sets has qualified this conclusion, demonstrating that life satisfaction does continue to rise with income, although each additional unit of income yields a progressively smaller improvement. The debate, in other words, is less about whether money matters than about how much it matters relative to other considerations.

Those other considerations turn out to be substantial. Studies consistently find that unemployment reduces well-being far more than the associated loss of income would predict, which implies that work provides purpose, structure and social contact as well as a wage. Lengthy commutes, chronic pain and loneliness are among the circumstances most strongly associated with low life satisfaction, while close relationships, good health and a sense of control over one's own life are among the most reliable predictors of high satisfaction. Notably, people appear to adapt quickly to many changes in material circumstances, so that a salary increase or a larger house delivers a boost that fades within a year or two, whereas they adapt only partially, if at all, to others, such as persistent noise or bereavement.

These findings have begun to influence public policy. Several national governments now publish official well-being statistics alongside conventional economic data, and at least one has introduced a budgetary process in which proposed expenditure must be assessed for its probable effect on citizens' well-being. Advocates contend that such an approach can redirect resources towards areas that conventional cost-benefit analysis tends to neglect, such as mental health services, which are relatively inexpensive yet, according to some estimates, generate greater gains in life satisfaction per unit of public money than almost any other intervention.

The approach is not without its detractors. Some maintain that self-reported happiness is too readily influenced by trivial factors, such as the weather on the day of the survey or the order in which questions are presented, to provide a sound basis for allocating public funds. Others raise a more philosophical objection: a government that sets out to maximise its citizens' happiness may be tempted to determine on their behalf what a good life consists of, and the pursuit of contentment could, in principle, be used to justify policies that discourage ambition or dissent. There is also a danger that a single well-being index, like GDP before it, comes to be treated as a target in its own right, encouraging policies that improve the measurement without improving the reality it is meant to reflect.

In my view, none of these objections is decisive. Survey responses are undoubtedly imperfect, but so is GDP, which is regularly revised by considerable margins years after its initial publication. The more persuasive conclusion is that no single figure can capture something as multifaceted as human welfare, and that governments should consult a range of indicators, both economic and subjective, while remaining candid about the limitations of each. Well-being data will not settle questions of value on our behalf. What they can do is ensure that those questions are asked.

tasks.prompt: The bar chart below shows the average number of hours per week that adults in one country spent on five leisure activities in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

visual.title: Average weekly hours spent on leisure activities by adults, 2005 and 2025

key_features: Overview: internet use replaced television as the most time-consuming activity; most other activities fell.
Internet use more than tripled, from 4 to 14.5 hours.
Television fell from 15.5 to 9 hours, losing its top position.
Meeting friends in person (8 to 5.5) and reading (4.5 to 2.5) both declined.
Sport and exercise was the only other activity to rise, slightly (3.5 to 4).
Total time on the five activities was unchanged at 35.5 hours; an answer must not claim an overall rise or fall.

model_answer.text:
The bar chart compares how many hours per week adults in one country devoted to five leisure activities in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, the most striking change was the shift from television to the internet: internet use, which was a minor pastime in 2005, had become the dominant leisure activity by 2025. Most other activities declined, with the exception of sport and exercise.

In 2005, watching television was by far the most popular activity, occupying an average of 15.5 hours a week, almost double the figure for meeting friends in person (8 hours). Adults spent only 4 hours online, slightly less than the time they spent reading (4.5 hours), while sport and exercise accounted for 3.5 hours.

Twenty years later, the picture had changed considerably. Time spent on the internet more than tripled to 14.5 hours, whereas television viewing fell by 6.5 hours to 9 hours a week. Meeting friends face to face and reading also became less common, dropping to 5.5 and 2.5 hours respectively. By contrast, sport and exercise rose marginally to 4 hours, making it the only activity apart from internet use to increase.

tasks.prompt: Some people believe that employees are more productive when they are allowed to work from home, while others argue that working in an office is better for both staff and the organisation. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
key_features: Discusses BOTH views with developed reasons (home: no commute, fewer interruptions, flexibility; office: collaboration, learning from colleagues, clear boundaries, team culture).
Gives a clear personal opinion in the introduction or conclusion and keeps it consistent.
Supports points with specific examples rather than general statements.
Clear paragraphing: introduction, one paragraph per view, opinion/conclusion.
Range of vocabulary on work (productivity, collaboration, commute, supervision) and accurate complex sentences.

model_answer.text:
Since the widespread adoption of video-conferencing tools, the question of where employees should work has become a matter of lively debate. While some argue that staff achieve more at home, others maintain that the office benefits both workers and their employers. In my view, the most effective arrangement combines the two.

Those in favour of home working point first to the time saved by not commuting. An employee who spends ninety minutes a day travelling can redirect that time to work or rest, arriving at the desk less tired and more focused. Home also offers fewer interruptions: tasks that require deep concentration, such as writing a report or analysing data, are often completed faster away from the noise of an open-plan office. Furthermore, the flexibility to organise one's day can improve motivation and reduce stress, particularly for parents.

On the other hand, the office has advantages that are difficult to reproduce online. Spontaneous conversations between colleagues frequently generate new ideas and solve problems in minutes that might otherwise take days of emails. Junior staff in particular learn a great deal simply by observing experienced colleagues, and they may struggle to develop professionally if they rarely meet them. There is also the question of boundaries: when the kitchen table becomes the workplace, many people find it hard to switch off, which can eventually lead to burnout.

In my opinion, both views contain an important truth, and organisations should therefore adopt a hybrid model. Focused individual work could be done at home on some days, while meetings, training and collaborative projects take place in the office on others. Such an approach allows companies to retain the benefits of teamwork without sacrificing the productivity and well-being gains of home working.

In conclusion, neither location is ideal for every task, and the most productive workplaces will be those that let the nature of the work decide where it is done.
